lesson.title: Fight or Flight: The Sympathetic Nervous System in Action
lesson.summary: This section explains the sympathetic nervous system, the branch of the autonomic nervous system that mobilizes the body for quick action under threat or stress, and why this response evolved.
lesson.body:
The sympathetic nervous system is one of the two branches of the autonomic nervous system introduced in the previous section, and its job is to prepare the body for action when it detects a threat or a stressful situation. This is the system responsible for what is commonly called the fight or flight response, a rapid, coordinated set of physical changes that gets the body ready either to confront a danger directly or to escape from it as quickly as possible.

When the sympathetic nervous system activates, it produces a cascade of physiological changes throughout the body, all pointed in the same direction: mobilizing energy for immediate physical action. Heart rate increases, pumping blood faster. Pupils dilate, letting in more light to sharpen vision. Blood flow shifts away from processes that are not immediately useful for survival, such as digestion, which slows down noticeably, and toward the skeletal muscles that would be needed to fight or run. The adrenal glands release stress hormones, including epinephrine, commonly known as adrenaline, into the bloodstream, which amplifies and sustains many of these changes. Breathing also quickens, delivering more oxygen to fuel the muscles that may be about to be called into action.

This response makes much more sense once connected back to the evolutionary perspective and natural selection covered earlier in this section. A fast, automatic threat response like this one would have been strongly favored by natural selection throughout human evolutionary history, since ancestors who could react to genuine danger, a predator, a physical attacker, almost instantly were more likely to survive long enough to reproduce than ancestors whose bodies reacted more slowly. Over countless generations, that survival advantage would have made a rapid sympathetic response increasingly common and eventually close to universal across the species, exactly the kind of process natural selection produces.

Consider a hiker who rounds a bend in a trail and suddenly spots what looks like a snake coiled a few feet ahead. Before the hiker has consciously finished processing what they are looking at, their heart is already pounding, their muscles have already tensed, and their body may have already begun to jump backward. The sympathetic nervous system acts that quickly precisely because, throughout evolutionary history, a threat response that waited for slow, deliberate conscious thought would often have arrived too late to matter.

The sympathetic nervous system essentially functions as the accelerator of the autonomic nervous system, and like any accelerator, it works best paired with a brake. That braking function belongs to its counterpart, the parasympathetic nervous system, which brings the body back down to a calm baseline once a threat has passed, and which is covered in full in the next section.
